review_text: Given the limitations of their performance venue, the technical presentation of Tullyvin Musical Society's production of 'The Addams Family' was nothing short of a minor miracle. To say there was a lack of space and facilities on and behind the stage would be an understatement, yet with good fore-thought, excellent stage management and a very capable building team, Tullyvin managed to extend their wing space, store a plethora of sizeable props and furniture, and present a stage that looked absolutely wonderful. The attention to detail in the house interior was unbelievable, with cobwebs, skulls, potions and abstract art, bannisters made of bones, candle-light, rickety stairs, portraits of the family and a collapsible wall with door frames and windows which then became the stage floor. It was all done in the worst possible taste and created the best possible effect. Simply ingenious. Visually spectacular.  Stage manager, Brian Feerick, had his work done in advance, and used cast members and costumed minions to carry out the furniture movement, and it all ran so smoothly. Whoever assembled the props for the show deserves a medal. They were plentiful and perfectly selected. The centre-stage trap door was well used, and the fold-down headstones were a clever touch. Gates and trees were enough to suggest different locations around the house. Having had the pleasure of visiting Tullyvin in the past, I am happy to report that this is a company very much in the ascendance, honing their skills, pushing themselves to higher levels of competence and confidence. 'The Addams Family' is pretty close to pantomime, with its surreal characters, un-likely plot, and abundantly ridiculous script, and it consequently takes a director with a zany, often outrageous, sense of humour to bring out the best in it. Such a director is Paul Norton who, from the get-go, used every conceivable gimmick, verbal and visual comedic device to enhance this piece to its fullness. From the highly amusing headstones that were on- stage as the audience entered, to the final note of the show, when Lurch managed, at last, to click his fingers in time with the rest of the cast, so much thought was put into the production. There was The Grim Reaper, who eerily ambled on stage, scythe in hand, to brief the audience on the emergency exits, and then assured them that they would be here for eternity. The audience were in the palm of their hands from that point onwards. Equally in tune with the production standards, Musical Director, John Roe, got us off to a rollicking good start with a lively and precisely played Overture, leading a very efficient six-piece band from the piano. He also maintained good contact with his on- stage performers throughout the show. If there were moments when one longed for more flamboyant dance routines, it was not the fault of choreographer, Julianne McNamara, but due to the absence of a male chorus. With what she had, Julianne worked hard to use the limited space effectively and with creativity, and the opening number, "When You're an Addams" was particularly impressive, and in fairness to the female chorus, they did all that was asked of them with a great sense of fun and an abundance of energy. Paul Norton not only directed, but also took on the role of Gomez, and led from the front, giving an inspirational performance. His comedy was of the highest order, but it was the sentiment and sincerity that he put into his relationships with Wednesday and Morticia that really made an impact, with "Happy, Sad" and "Live Before We Die" providing the emotional high-points of the show. Excellent work. Andrea Fitzpatrick was a confident and convincing Morticia, with good vocal quality and a fine sense of comic timing. She had the strength of character to keep Gomez on his toes, but also the grace and gentleness to see the errors of her stubbornness. A powerful vocal quality was the highlight of a very assured performance from Emily Smith as Wednesday Addams. She maintained a delightful dead-pan throughout the show, which contrasted brilliantly with the joy in her vocals. Sean Slowey had attitude and presence as the masochistic young Pugsley. He looked the part, nailed his comedy, and delivered his vocals with confidence. Standing at approximately 8', Jason Nulty was certainly the tallest Lurch I've ever encountered, and fair play to him for his relaxed confidence on those stilts, but his height was overshadowed by his equally enormous personality, which shone through a wonderful comedic performance. In contrast, it was the amiable, somewhat demented smile of Liam Wallace's Fester that made him so appealing. He flirted delightfully with the audience and made the most of his musical numbers, especially "The Moon and Me". This was a most note-worthy comedic performance. Emma McKeown worked hard and was impressive in the role of Grandma, but even with good make-up and wig, she couldn't completely disguise that she was a bit too young for the role. John Grogan, as Mal Beineke, probably needed to be more authoritative in his early scenes, but he came good when he relaxed into his old self as the show progressed. Pamela McCormack got a good contrast between her nervous wife of the early scenes and her more provocative vamp of the Full Disclosure scene. The Beinekes were a little pitchy vocally in the difficult "Crazier Than You" number, but they were a capable and entertaining couple nevertheless. As their son, Lucas, Colm Shalvey was well partnered with Wednesday, nerdy enough to frustrate her, and yet confident enough to win her over in the end. A well- judged performance with a good confident singing voice. An uncredited Grim Reaper brought a captivating start to the show and was useful throughout in assisting with furniture moves. The vocal quality of the female chorus was good and their actions and reactions were a good contributing factor to the flow and ambiance of their many scenes. Costumes throughout were entirely appropriate and well presented. Chorus greys were effective, combined with good ghostly make-up and an assortment of very good wigs and hairstyles. Lurch's extended physique (approx. 8' high) was very well achieved, looked proportioned, and was excellently used by the actor. It was the combination of all the above with the superbly dressed set that made this show an absolute visual treat, and all comments made about the effort made on presenting a visually exceptional set can be extended to include the effort that went into the dressing of the front of house area. A lovely Halloween atmosphere was created, and front of house staff were delightful, helpful and most welcoming. I think the most evident characteristic of this production was the sheer sense of fun and enjoyment that emanated from the stage, which I have little doubt was contributed to by the influence and personality of their Director. The overall performance level was high, often hilarious, and always thoroughly entertaining. Congratulations on a most enjoyable experience. It was a very great pleasure to be with you.

society_raw: North East Music & Dramatic Society, Castleblayney
review_text: Whether It's always exciting to see a new musical society pop on to the radar, but it's uncommon for them to explode onto the radar to such an extent that one has to adjust all the settings and brace oneself for a veritable roller-coaster ride from the opening chorus to the final curtain. But this was exactly the impact created by the highly talented cast and production team of the North East Musical and Dramatic Society's production of "9 to 5". Attention to detail was the key to the high sheen that made this such a polished production. Director, Gavin Quigley, had a talented cast to work with, and he complemented them by providing well- paced, easy-flowing action, with a strong focus on comedy. Principals were always comfortable on the stage, and there was good attention to the smaller character roles, making their performances stand out and relevant. Excellent work. I was blown away by the energy and the precision of the dance routines throughout the show. Moreover, they weren't just dances. They always had a purpose and contributed to the story line. The opening chorus was a masterpiece of non-stop, stylised, scene-setting, performed by a dynamic and extremely energetic ensemble, which led almost seamlessly into an equally exciting "Around Here." The entire Dream sequence, from "Dance of Death" through to "Joy to the Girls" was meticulous, creative, inspirational and thoroughly engaging, as was the "Shine Like The Sun" finale to Act One. "One of the Boys" set the second act alight, and the terpsichorean treat never waned until the rousing finale. This was top notch choreography, brought to life by a skilled and spirited group of performers. Choreographer, Leah Meagher, take a bow. The show was very well costumed, and I noted the lovely change, when Violet and the girls took over the running of the office, to brighter and more colourful outfits. Good costumes for the Dream sequence dance routines and for One of the Boys. Wigs and Hairstyles were always appropriate, and make-up looked natural throughout. Carol McCourt was a worthy Violet Newstead, brimming with confidence, displaying great leadership quality, and as strong in her vocals as she was in her acting. Her comedy was very well timed, and she fronted her musical numbers with a reassuring ease. Louise Steele was a robust Doralee, delightfully voluptuous and self-assured, yet soft and gentle when it was required. Her delivery of Backwoods Barbie was particularly endearing. As with Carol, her vocal quality matched her acting skills. Completing the main trio, Paige Kelly was a perfect choice for the role of Judy, vulnerable and insecure, yet when it was required, thoroughly capable of making a powerful impact. Her "Get Out and Stay Out" was one of the musical highlights of the show. Sean Harkin gave a top-drawer performance as the misogynist boss, Franklin Hart Jnr, enjoying every moment of the comedy, and performing his songs with great energy. He was delightfully loathsome in all his dealings with his female staff, and we were truly delighted to see him getting his come-uppance at the end. Lorraine Cotter was obnoxiously authoritative as Roz Keith, and divinely comedic in her lust for Franklin. "Heart to Hart" was very well performed, and I think we all felt a little sorry for her when she was sent away to learn French. James Brennan was a very likeable and sympathetic Joe, firm but gentle in his love for Violet, and his singing in "Let Love Grow" was very pleasant indeed. Orla Sheridan made an excellent comedic contribution to the show as the office lush, Margaret, growling through her drunken haze and ultimately returning from rehab as an articulate and sophisticated lady. Strong support came from Sinead Walshe as Maria, Fiona Longmuir as Missy and Lauren Murphy as Kathy, all of whom established themselves as individuals. Calum Duffy played teenage son, Josh, with a relaxed confidence, while Adam Lynagh as Dwayne and Thomas Whyte as Dick gave solid support in their respective roles. There were good performances too from Aoibheann Byrne, Emma Kerley, Kerrie Gorman, Issac John, and new-comer Peter Phillips made an excellent job of his maiden performance as Tinsworthy. In their vocal contributions, in the execution of their numerous dance routines and in their top-notch reacting to the focal point of the action, the chorus were the backbone of this production. They were meticulously attired, energetic and brimming with expression and confidence. With four people credited as Musical Director, Chorus Mistress/Mister, it's hard to know who did what in preparation of the musical content of the show, but it's safe to say that a mountain of work was done on achieving a strong and harmonious choral sound. Musical entrances and cut- offs were all precisely timed, which was a good achievement without the benefit of a conductor out front to keep control. This brings me appropriately to the drawbacks of using backing tracks. There were a few occasions when the stage team were so efficient with their scene changes that there was a surplus of music that we had to endure in darkness before the lights took us into the next scene. There was one obvious and a couple of minor incidents when principals got through their dialogue briskly and were left with a lengthy pause of inactivity before their vocal cue. I acknowledge that these flaws were highlighted by the fact that the rest of the show was so perfectly paced. Setting the level of the backing tracks can also cause concern, and while volume wasn't a problem, there was a pounding bass throughout the show that made the output unnecessarily heavy and rattled the eardrums a little. That said, it was most enjoyable to hear a full orchestra sound at an affordable cost. Lighting was varied and atmospheric, with excellent use of the louvered light boxes. Lighting cues were crisp and precise, and only on a few occasions were the chorus a tad too dimly lit behind a highlighted principal. Sound quality throughout, (apart from that bass line) was very good, including the video voice-overs. As already mentioned, the stage sets were clean and beautifully presented, with very good props and furniture, and all managed and moved by cast and crew with mega-efficiency, under the guidance of the director, who also doubled as stage manager. After an arduous journey from Galway to Castleblayney, it was lovely to receive such a warm welcome to the beautiful Iontas Theatre. Front of House manager, Monica Marron, and her staff were delightful and efficient and their hospitality was generous. This really was an excellent night of entertainment from a fresh and exciting new musical group. My sincere thanks to you all for a most uplifting and thoroughly enjoyable experience. I hope you continue to produce and present such a high calibre of musical entertainment.

As I left An Tain Arts Centre in Dundalk last night, I overheard a conversation between two teenagers. "That was pretty good," said one, "but I didn't know any of the songs." "I knew the one that the girl who sounded like Forest Gump sang," said the other. "I can't say No. I think I've heard Ma singin' that to me Da." Lucky man, thinks myself. My wife says no to me all the time, but that's neither here nor there. The point is that Oklahoma despite its age, still has an appeal to a generation who have never seen nor heard of it before, which is probably why it remains such a popular choice for musical societies throughout the country. And when a production is as well manicured as this one was, it's easy to understand its popularity. Trimming the fat, would be an apt description of Director, Tony Finnegan's approach to the show. "It's a Scandal" was gone (no great loss) and some irrelevant dialogue as the show reached its climax, resulting in a more fluid journey to the final rousing chorus. Tony's trademark is to include children in his productions, and whether they are needed or not, it does add authenticity to crowd scenes to see family units enjoying themselves. Moreover, he also used them in this production to create a beautiful ballet scene that saw Curly and Laurey playing together as children. This was a lovely detail. The pace throughout the show was very good, and relationships were all very believable. There was good chemistry between Curly and Laurey, and between Ado Annie and both Will and Ali. Good tension was created in the scenes involving Jud Fry, and there were nicely added comedic touches that added a freshness to the well tried and tested script. What the show definitely had was confidence, engagement and great attention to detail, all of which suggest a thoroughly rehearsed and well-thought out production. Musically, the show was a treat. In the safe hands of Musical Director, Ronan Dennedy, we were treated to a nicely balanced and precisely performed accompaniment from the orchestra throughout the show, and an equally accomplished vocal performance from the entire cast. Credit goes to Chorus Mistress, Ann McCabe for a well-drilled and thoroughly rehearsed chorus. As Curly McClain, Ray O'Hare sang in the most delightful tones, and proved to be a confident and capable actor. His relationship with Laurey was always playful, romantic and sincere, and he showed no fear when standing up to the ogre-ish Jud. This was a well-judged performance. Clara Quigley, as Laurey, had an equally pleasant singing voice, and a delightful coquettishness in her flirting with Curly. She handled her fear of Jud extremely well up to the point where she eventually admonishes his behaviour, when she was, perhaps, almost too strong. Nevertheless, this was a very capable all-round performance. As Ado Annie, Chloe Copas managed to wring every ounce of comedy out of her character. He vocal delivery, her facial expressions and her body language all came together to create an engaging and loveable caricature to which the audience certainly warmed very quickly. As for her accent, well, it certainly made me laugh, even if it jarred slightly with all around her. It was the exuberance of youth that made Max Valentine's Will Parker so likeable. His comedy was perhaps a little over-emphasised, but his energy was infectious, and this is a young comedian to watch out for in the future. His singing was very good and his dancing was, well…enthusiastic and very entertaining. I enjoyed the performance of David McArdle as Ali Hakim, who had more than a touch of Benny Hill about both his physical and vocal comedy. His timing was very good and he handled the added "Hakim v Hakeeeem" gag with accomplishment. He was a very enjoyable likeable-rogue. Confidence and security under-pinned the delightful performance of Patricia Savage in the role of Aunt Eller. There was the warmth of her care and concern for Laurey, and humorous teasing of Curly in his romantic endeavours. She also fronted "The Farmer and the Cowman" and the auction scene with authority. James McGinn's Jud Fry was menacing, but showed signs of a psychopathic nature with his almost childlike tantrums and explosive temperament. His scene with Curly in the smoke-house was particularly well-judged. This was a strong performance and his passionate deliver of "Lonely Room" completely validated his vocal credibility after a slight hiccup at the end of "Poor Jud". Tim Ahern was an amusing and very credible Andrew Carnes, clear and sharp in his delivery of dialogue. He was well supported by Aaron Matthews as Cord Elam, Eoghan Weldon as Slim and Stephen Clarke as Ike Skidmore, who all gave individuality to their characters. As Gertie Cummings, Caoimhe McBride was suitably pert and pretentious, and enhanced her performance with a truly irritating laugh/giggle. Nicely played. A special mention for Josh Murphy, Aoife O'Connor, Eoghan Weldon (again) and Leah Kearney, as the Younger Curlys and Laureys, who delightfully contributed to the show, particularly during the ballet. And speaking of the ballet, choreographer, Sinéad Lightley-Collins, broke with tradition here by introducing young Curly and young Laurey, playing together as children, and then progressing through generations up to the characters of the present. It was a delightful distraction and enhanced the usual nightmare scenario. "The Farmer and the Cowman" had a good natural flow to it, with good patterns and precise movement, even if it wasn't as rambunctious as one might have expected. Kansas City was not overly ambitious, but was enthusiastically performed. The ensemble were clearly well-rehearsed in their musical pieces, showing good strength and wonderful harmonies. The picture finish of "The Farmer and the Cowman" allowed the vocal quality to shine, and it certainly did. The Oklahoma Chorus was equally pleasant to listen to, and the ladies made a very good job of "Many A New Day" and "Out of My Dreams". Chorus action and reaction throughout the show was very believable and dances were always tidy and precise, thanks to good choreography that took heed of the performers' capabilities. Played on a well-designed and wood- stained set, incorporating an attractive gauze curtain, scene changes, in the capable hands of Stage Manager, Niall McCooey, were managed with a minimum of fuss. There were plenty of well-selected props and furniture pieces, including a decidedly grubby and effective smoke- house for Jud. The symbolic creation of a surrey, using bales of hay, cartwheels and a canopy, was a clever device to negate the need for a full surrey on stage for the finale. Lighting was often atmospheric and generally well-illuminated, but there were a few instances of lights flickering on and off, which occasionally distracted from the action. The end of the ballet, with highlights on the young couple and the dropped Rose, was reminiscent of Beauty and the Beast, but nonetheless, very effective. Sound quality was very good, and apart from an occasional moment of feed-back, every word was clearly heard. Sound effects, especially the gun-shots, were very well timed. Costumes for the show were appropriate and utilitarian, as opposed to over-stylised, which is a break from the abundance of ginghams and bright colours that we so often see in this musical, but all the more authentic for that. There was a bit of variation in hem lengths for the ladies dresses, and indeed, one or two modern fringes in hairstyles, but aside from those minor indiscretions, the show was visually very tidily presented. Wigs were appropriate and worn well, and make-up was natural and very satisfactory. Principal costumes were very good, particularly the ladies, and Ali Hakim was appropriately more garish and gaudy than those around him. In safe hands, Oklahoma! will always be an entertaining show, but in creative hands, it can be enhanced and delivered with a freshness that draws in a new generation to appreciate the genius of this Rogers and Hammerstein classic. Congratulations to Tony and to all in Dundalk for achieving that goal, and for a thoroughly enjoyable night of musical theatre.

One Normal Night Full disclosure: this musical totally undermines the whole concept of the Addams Family being weird by making them aspire to normality. Morticia doesn't want to grow old, Wednesday wants to get married, Gomez wants peace and harmony in his family and even the ghosts and ghouls, the family's ancestors, want normality for their descendants. The only characters who in any way remain true to the original conceit are Grandma Addams and Pugsley who misses his sister torturing him. Even Fester wants to live happily ever after, albeit with the moon as his significant other. So, if you are a fan of Charles Addams' work, you will be confused. The Addams family, led by the elegantly black-clad Morticia, a wonderfully still Leah Penston, and her ever-devoted amorous husband Gomez, an ebullient Fergal Millar, is unsettled. Their daughter Wednesday, a bob-haired Leah Comerford, now eighteen, finds herself falling in love and considering marriage, which she is keeping from her mother but confesses to her Dad. When she invites her new boyfriend, Lucas Beineke, the wonderful Simon Broderick, and his family over for dinner to their gothic house of horrors, it turns out that the 'normal' family are even more messed up than the Addams. It's quite a simple plot worthy of an American rom-com, but the jokes are good, and the performances fresh and narrator Fester ensures that it we don't take it too seriously as he constantly reminds us that we are watching a musical. Director Christine Scarry pulled out all the stops together with Musical Director, David Hayes and Choreographer Nicole McDonald and gave us a physically reduced version of the show due to the limitations of the stage, but a production full of talent and a few surprises! This is a huge musical and the challenge was considerable to fit it all in on the Watergate stage. The Addams' house should be massive with hidden and secret passages and doors and picture frames for the Ancestors to pop out of, and we did get some of this in John O'Donoghue's clever set. Most notable was the internally lit trap up stage right, which was very effective, especially when Pugsley used it, and the stairs leading up to an impressively high landing. The projections of skeletal tree branches added a menace to a show that isn't very scary and Terry Heron's sound effects were brilliant, lots of loud thunder and crash, bangs and wallops which created jump scares for the audience. Colm Eaton's lighting was hauntingly beautiful at times with some lovely blues. The father of the snap-happy Addams Family is Gomez, here played by Fergal Simon Broderick as the loved-up Lucas and Leah Comerford as the crazy Wednesday Addams fabulous as he sashayed around the stage wooing his deadpan wife. Leah Penston's Morticia was an exercise in less is more. Communicating her thoughts or contempt or pleasure with an elegant flick of her wrist, Ms Penston didn't have to try. Her voice was exquisite on all her numbers but particularly on "Just Around the Corner" and her duet with Gomez "Live Before we Die" and her dancing was equally adept. Their daughter, Wednesday, was played by Leah Comerford with a goth- like sensibility, slamming around the stage moaning that her parents didn't understand her. She had this thousand- yard stare throughout the show that hinted at her being slightly unhinged, a trait that clearly attracted Lucas her fiancé, who was wonderfully played by Simon Broderick with a boy-next-door ambiance. Mr Broderick has a sweet voice, which he used to great effect on "Crazier Than You" with Ms Comerford. She also sang well on "Pulled" accompanied by her brother Pugsley's ecstatic groans as she tortured him. Ms Comerford had a good chemistry with Ciarán O'Dwyer's Pugsley, who was just the perfect evil little brother. Mischievous and conniving, he steals a truth potion from his Grandma, a hilarious Claire Henriques who resembled Brenda Fricker from Home Alone 2, to administer to Wednesday but inadvertently it is given to Lucas' Mother, Alice during the family game "Full Disclosure" and all hell breaks loose. Alice, here played wonderfully by Sarah Brennan, a typical suburban Mom in a loveless marriage devotes her life to her son, Lucas. Ms Brennan captured her essence perfectly, when her rhyming couplets and forced laughter exploded into a rant about her life in the stunning "Waiting", which brought the house down. Her self-absorbed husband, Mal was played by Jody Ridgwell with a delicious cynicism. Both sang well on "Crazier Than You" with Wednesday and Lucas. The Addams butler, Lurch, was played by Mark Duffy. I loved Mr Duffy's physical comedy. His slowness as Lurch really worked for the character as did his moans and groans. Non-verbal characters are difficult to do in a show, but he did it very well. However, the star of the show was David Doyle's Uncle Fester, brother to Gomez. This performance was at another level. From his aggressive gaze out to the audience at the start to his playfulness with the Ancestors and the audience, Mr Doyle owned the stage. This was not the Fester we are used to. Ms Scarry and Mr Doyle took a chance in contemporising the character and it worked brilliantly. He had the audience in the palm of his hand, and they perked up whenever he entered. His energy and stagecraft were exceptional as he swaggered across the stage throughout. "The Moon and Me", where he declared his love for Luna, was ridiculously sweet but he made it work as we wanted him to find love. The audience crooned "Ahh…", when he set off on his journey to his paramour strapped to some very hazardous looking rockets at the end of the show. Everyone was on the same page in this show, which is sadly not often the case in some productions. They clearly understood the genre and the director's vision. When they broke the fourth wall (particularly Fester & Gomez), they did it within the spirit of the show and did not pantomime it - they were always in control. As a cohesive ensemble, the Ancestors were always attentive to the 'Family' and did not stray their focus. Christine Scarry directed a slick, fast paced show which was loud and proud and took no prisoners. Some lovely moments of theatre during the show; like Fester's use and abuse of the exercise ball, the penetrating gaze of the Family during "When You're an Addams", the inventive set and exquisite lighting. Her work with the cast, and especially the principals was clever and delicate, which I think, made them feel invested in the production. Her Ancestors were always on point and never wavered. Ms Scarry's interpretation of the work was measured and accurate with a few adroit little changes and she also took risks, which made it a very good show.

Lost in the Darkness It may seem an odd choice to create a musical based on Robert Louis Stevenson's gothic horror novella written in 1886. But Frank Wildhorn did just that in 1990 and like most musicals it went through a series of re-writes until it hit Broadway in 1997 and with another re-write, on tour in the UK in 2004. Wildhorn is clearly attracted to the dark side of human nature having also written musicals based on Dracula and The Count of Monte Cristo among many others. Jekyll and Hyde has quite a dense and overblown operatic score and seems heavily influenced by Les Miserables and especially The Phantom of the Opera. But, it also has a charm of its own and features some great tunes. Bravo Theatre Group, based in Loughrea in Galway, staged the show in the Temperance Hall in late September, early October this year. Directed and choreographed by long-time Bravo collaborator, Aoife McClafferty, with musical direction by the ubiquitous Shane Farrell, this was on the surface, the ideal production for the talented Bravo team, who often tackle difficult shows. The plot follows Dr Henry Jekyll, who vows to explore and excise the darkness within man through chemical means by experimenting on human subjects. The Board of Governors in the hospital where he practices won't allow this, so he experiments on himself by drinking a serum he's concocted. This has disastrous consequences as he releases his alter ego, Mr Hyde who rampages ripper-like through Victorian London. Interestingly, Jekyll is a not a very nice character, being self-obsessed and narcissistic but also a bit simpering. Hyde, in contrast was written as a charming psychopathic murderer and it could be argued that his killing of certain characters was vigilantism (the pederast bishop for instance). Leading the cast was Stephen Rabbette as Jekyll/Hyde in a role that is not for the faint-hearted or the novice. It requires enormous stamina, a powerful voice and serious acting chops to pull it off. Mr Rabbette is certainly no novice having been in plenty of productions down through the years and it showed. His stagecraft was excellent as was his vocal. He effortlessly switched between roles, often quite quickly like during 'Transformation' where he sings as both characters. Lucy, a prostitute Jekyll befriends at the notorious Red Rat underground club/ brothel, where she is the main attraction was played with self-confidence by Sarah Corcoran. Ms Corcoran's portrayal of Lucy was interesting in that her Lucy yearns for something better in her life and fantasises about Jekyll possibly 'taking her away from all of this' yet is attracted to Hyde. Hyde visited Lucy many times at the Red Rat eventually killing her as she intended to leave him and London. Ms Corcoran sang exquisitely on 'Bring on the Men' and her duets with both Emma (Jekyll's fiancé) and Nellie (another Red Rat employee) were highlights of the show. Nellie was played beautifully by Emily Lohan in a stand-out performance full of character and distinction and one of the few characters who sang in dialect. The illicit drinking den was run by a sleezy pimp called Spider, performed by Fergal D'Arcy in long coat and faux dreads, who exuded menace and viciousness particularly in his violent scene with Lucy. Emma Danvers, Jekyll's clueless fiancé, was played by Emer Kelly who had a fine classical voice. Her duet with Jekyll 'Take Me as I am' was lovely as was her solo 'Once Upon a Dream'. However, it was her duet with Lucy 'In His Eyes' where she could really let go and she was fabulous. Her father, Sir Danvers, Chair of the Board of Governors - a nice performance by Declan Kelly - believes in Jekyll and wants to help him but is also concerned about whether he's the right man for his daughter. Other members of the Board, who rejected Jekyll's experiments were: Tomás Glynn, very strong as Simon Fergal D'Arcy playing the creepy Spider and Sarah Corcoran playing Lucy in Bravo Theatre Group's Jekyll and Hyde Stride who disliked Jekyll and had designs on Emma; Michelle Drysdale as Lady Beaconsfield in a superbly notable performance; Cian O'Ceallaigh suitably boorish as Sir Archibald Proops; Declan Finn as General Lord Glossop; Jonathan Hopper as the lascivious Bishop of Basingstoke and David O'Grady in a finely judged performance as Lord Savage. All were perfectly cast and excelled in 'Bitch, Bitch, Bitch' which some were in and 'Board of Governors' where they worked wonderfully well together. Jekyll's long-suffering lawyer friend, John Utterson, who narrates the novella, and the opening of this show was played by Norman Quinn with a geniality and showed great emotion at his friend's descent to what he assumes is madness. Jekyll's servant, Poole, was nicely played by Oisin Dowling and the apothecary, Bisset by a laconic Larry Morgan. In the final scene, the wedding, officiated by a very funny John Hayes as the Priest, when Jekyll finally seemed to have shaken off the demon, Hyde returned and rather than have Emma suffer in his hands, commits suicide. The ensemble voices and movement on the various 'Façade', 'Bitch, Bitch, Bitch' and 'Murder, Murder' were fabulous. Really strong, with great harmonies and especially fine sopranos. These scenes were a joy to hear and a special mention must go to Megan Lohan, who never lost character throughout these scenes. It's not a big dance show, but there are some movement scenes like the ones above and a Fosse style 'Bring on the Men' led by Lucy, which was like a Kit Kat Klub number from Cabaret but very well danced by the ensemble. Choreographer, Aoife McClafferty clearly spent a lot of time on all these scenes because they were quite flawlessly executed and worked. Shane Farrell's musical direction was also faultless. His work with the ensemble voices was gorgeous, we could hear every harmony and his band were super. Derek Reck's sound helped here, pushing the sound out to us, delicate and at times booming, particularly Hyde's reverbed Phantomesque laugh. Paul Kelly's lighting was so good it seemed organic in that it seemed to grow with the scenes, out of John Wright's super moody set. Nomac's costumes were of good quality and Ali Murphy's wigs suitable, particularly Jekyll's wig. Clodagh Farrell stage managed this big show on a small stage with professionalism and her transitions were smooth. Jekyll and Hyde is a flawed work, the lib is a bit creaky and it doesn't always make sense. Some of the music can be mawkish and the ending is awful. However, Aoife McClafferty and Bravo brought a freshness to the piece helped by a superb cast, orchestra and dedicated creatives that made it work. A well- deserved standing ovation by the audience capped off a very entertaining evening of theatre.

Rebel Without a Crew Originally called 'Can't Help Falling in Love', the title was changed by the writer to 'All Shook Up' because it was apparently easier to remember which helps with marketing. Written by Joe DiPietro, who borrowed shamelessly from William Shakespeare and featuring music made popular by Elvis Presley, 'All Shook Up' is a true jukebox musical set in a small-town in USA in the fifties. It even had a jukebox spot lit in pre- set on the stage of the Market Place Theatre in Armagh where I saw it in early October. Produced by Banbridge Musical Society and directed by Ian Milford, this post-modern show also borrows from 'Footloose' and 'Grease' as we follow the citizens of 'nowhereville' as they try to come to grips with their feelings of love and romance awakened by a highly sexed stranger who rides into town. Chad, played brilliantly by Daniel May, arrives in town on his malfunctioning motorbike looking for a mechanic, having just been released from prison in another state. He meets Natalie, winningly played by Emma McGuckin, the local grease monkey, and she becomes smitten. Chad however only has eyes for Miss Sandra, a feisty Claire Costello, the intellectual caretaker of the local museum. Natalie dresses as a guy to get her guy a la 'Twelfth Night' and the other townsfolk all fall for each other. That's the plot. I Emma McGuckin as the smitten Natalie and Daniel May as the handsome Chad in Banbridge Mus. Society's All Shook Up mean it's hardly Shakespeare...oh hang on, it is! However, in some ways the plot is unimportant as it's merely there to showcase the songs. The story is wafer thin, but it can be very funny when executed properly. Basically, this is a farce, and each joke or situation should be milked for all it's worth for it to work. It shouldn't be taken seriously and indeed relishes in its own self-parody. Thankfully, director Ian Milford and his talented cast and creatives knew this and what we got was a hilarious rom-com set to some great tunes, orchestrated by Niall O'Flaherty, and interspersed with a lot of high-energy dance numbers choreographed by Jordan Rosborough. The set, by Theatrical Sets Ireland, was bright and cheery, with an almost high- school musical vibe in its celebration of kitsch. Rosemary Kelly's costumes included typical 1950's garb but also featured some abundant angels and devils (in disguise) and a plethora of blue suede shoes and wedding gowns. Lighting by Rodney Ellis was suitably garish and sound by Enda McClusker was full range with lots of sound effects. Stage Manager Andrew McKnight marshalled his crew and cast with a firm hand on the hi-jinks so that everything went where it should, when it should. Mr Milford's cast were full of energy and drew the audience into this weird and wonderful cartoon world. Everyone on the stage shone with excitement, high on the adrenaline rush of performance, infecting the audience with glee. Mr May's Chad sang with passion and danced with hip- thrusting abandon throughout the show, Ms McGuckin's Natalie also sang with, at times, poignancy and joy and her alter- ego 'Ed' was perfectly judged. Their duet "Follow That Dream" was very sweet. Jordan Walsh played Natalie's friend, Dennis, who is secretly in love with her. Mr Walsh made this role his own, a bumbling, nerdy character who yearns to be like Chad but physically just can't compete. His performance was a masterclass in comic timing and his voice on "It Hurts Me" was quite moving. The local honky-tonk, 'Sylvia's' is where much of the action in Act 1 takes place. This is run by, you've guessed it, Sylvia who was played by Maille Connolly. She is a single parent bringing up her daughter Lorraine, a 16 year-old bobby soxer played wonderfully by Aimee McVeigh. Both performers had a nice harmony together and were quite believable as mother and daughter. Ms Connolly sang with a lot of jazz/blues emotion on "There's Always Me" a song about her unrequited love for Jim, Natalie's father whilst Ms McVeigh sang with gusto on "It's Now or Never" with Dean, her soon to be boyfriend played with a smart Mummy's boy air by Shane Curran. Sylvia's crush and Natalie's father, Jim, was played Ruairi McAlinden. This was the performance of the show for me. He not only sang brilliantly but had a magnificent naturalism on stage, was totally convincing as the widower, full of sorrow yet wanted to move on with his life. Lovely work and all hidden, as it should be. This odd little town was full of offbeat, weird characters. The town's mayor, Mayor Matilda Hyde was indeed a monstrous Hyde-like character, outlawing "loud music, public necking, and tight pants." Magnificently played by Jacqueline Mathews, she chewed the scenery and spat it out at everyone, especially her sidekick the silent Sheriff Earl, played with mute fury by David McClelland. Ms Mathews was a Scooby- Doo baddie, singing "(You're the) Devil in Disguise" about her arch nemesis Chad, with a chorus of Angels and Devils accompanying her. A perfectly pitched comic performance. Another pivotal character was Miss Sandra, curator of the town's museum, and a rural Miss Moneypenny, all glasses and tight-fitting dress. She sang well on "Let Yourself Go" accompanied by her moving statues, in a surreal scene with Natalie. In Act 2, the action moved to the abandoned funfair on the outskirts of town. This was where it became really farcical, with lots of entrances and exits, falling down, Chad questioning his sexuality when he kissed 'Ed', Matilda wanting Earl to shoot everyone, her son defying her and so on. It was pure madcap and slapstick. But it worked as it was so well choreographed. Director, Ian Milford let loose, and the tongues became firmly embedded in each character's cheek. Of course, all's well that ends well, and everyone got the one that they wanted and deserved. Natalie found her feministic side and Chad, relieved that 'Ed' was a girl, became her sidekick. Dennis and Miss Sandra discovered they had a mutual love for poetry, particularly Shakespeare's sonnets, Lorraine and Dean hooked up with his mother's blessing and Jim and Sylvia also tied the knot. Earl finally spoke up and proposed to Matilda and they all lived happily ever after. Comedy is very difficult to do well. Farce is even more demanding as it is mostly physical and is totally reliant on timing, and each performer must play everything totally seriously. Banbridge Musical Society under Ian Milford's astute direction nailed the comedy in this show whilst showcasing some delightful voices and clever choreography that went beyond the usual for a 1950's set show.

The Addams Family is all about fun and ridiculous comedy, and these are the elements that the St.Patrick's production rightly focused on. With a talented front- line at his disposal, Director, Simon Pyper, provided a no-nonsense approach to the show, making sure the story was told at a brisk pace and with plenty of activity to keep the audience interested. I liked his use of living photo frames throughout the show, which worked particularly well when Morticia discussed her family album. The chorus of dead ancestors were a nice addition to virtually every scene, as if they had a right to be there, but they needed to take care not to pull focus from the dialogue. Good attention was given to characterisation throughout the cast, each having a definite individuality, and most achieving a high level of performance. Having a good grounding in pantomime, I was delighted to see Simon putting good emphasis on the slap-stick, visual comedy aspects of the show. Overall, a very nice package. While the set was well painted, well designed and very functional, the front areas were perhaps less effective in detail, Pugsley's torture "rack" could have been a tad more inventive, and the chair might have been a bit more terrifying. The available space was, however, well used. The use of laurel branches as the forest was very effective. Lighting was generally quite good, although on occasions, the follow spot could have been intensified. Also, the monster in Pugsley's bedroom was almost lost in darkness. There were issues with Mal's microphone which took some time to resolve, but the sound and effects were generally good. Alex McFarlane did a good job of creating exciting dance routines, and of highlighting her best dancers. The front line were very capable and precise, but the full chorus also proved to be high achievers in their movement. They were also very accomplished vocally. With a tight six piece band under him, Musical Director, Wilson Shields, controlled both the musicians and the on-stage singers with precision and good balance. Principals and Chorus seemed well-rehearsed and all made a most pleasing sound. Musically, the show was extremely secure. I'm starting to suspect that Sean Harkin has a double, for he seems to be popping up everywhere. Last week he starred in 9 to 5 in Co. Monaghan, and now he's playing the lead in The Addams Family in Downpatrick. Such energy and enthusiasm are undoubtedly the reason why he performs like a Duracell Bunny, always animated and always on top of his game. His Gomez had pace and a wacky personality that gave it a cartoon quality, and yet he handled his sympathetic scenes with Wednesday and Morticia most sincerely. A nicely balanced performance with impressive vocals thrown in for good measure. Jordan Rosborough was the definitive Morticia. Venomous when crossed, vampish and vivacious when inspired, she commanded the stage with her very appearance. Her singing was as strong on interpretation of the lyrics as it was on vocal quality, making 'Death is Just Around The Corner' a divine performance piece. Her comedy was of the finest quality. Truly her mother's daughter, there were similar qualities on display from Fiona Rice as Wednesday. This was a young performer full of promise, who looked, reacted and sang most impressively throughout. It was hard to believe that this was her first principal role. Uncle Fester was well played by an energetic Andrew Devonshire, who, as narrator, made a good connection with the audience. What he lacked in vocal quality, he made up for with good interpretation, although 'The Moon and Me', while nicely danced, was a little disjointed. His comedic timing was on point. Maya Kelly was a feisty Pugsley, full of outward attitude, yet soft in the centre, and we loved that under the bravado, she just wanted to be loved/tortured by her sister. Nicely played. Kathryn Anne Simpson's Grandma was quite a gentle soul, which made her moments of ribald humour all the more comical and unexpected. A better wig would have enhanced her appearance and aged her more convincingly. Aaron McElroy's Lurch possibly needed to be more visually intimidating to create a stronger impact, but he did all that was asked of him with good confidence and security. Laoise Carney was a rather reserved Alice Beineke, which served her well in her early scenes, but she needed to be slightly more 'unrestrained' in her 'disclosure' scenes. But she and her husband combined beautifully with Wednesday and Lucas in a fine rendition of the musically tricky "Crazier Than You" number. Tim Pentland was most impressive as Mal Beineke, a suitable stuffed-shirt in his early scenes and convincingly 'hip' when he rediscovered his former self. Very nicely played. Adam Madine captured the character of Lucas extremely well, proving to be a worthy partner for Wednesday and singing with confidence throughout. The variety of characters among the ancestors was excellent, each with a very eye-catching costume to suit. Lovely detail. Chorus were really well dressed, their make-up was creative and their hairstyles and wigs were appropriate and well worn. The show was visually interesting and well-designed. This was a production that tickled me in so many places, and while it's easy to nit-pick a production that is generally of a high standard, the most important feature of any show is the impact it has on the audience. The Downpatrick audiences loved it, so congratulations to one and all for a ridiculous and highly entertaining night of ghoulish fun. Thanks also to Anne Millar and the front of house team for the warm hospitality and refreshments.

For those who may not have seen the movie upon which this new musical is based, Nativity, not surprisingly, tells the story of a reluctant primary teacher's attempts to put on a nativity show, haunted by the fact that his previous effort, some years earlier, had been a total disaster. When he is pressured into it, he has a new employee, Mr Poppy, thrust upon him as an assistant. But Mr Poppy is not your conventional classroom assistant. To say that he is child-like and unpredictable would be an understatement, but he is the catalyst for the mayhem and madness that brings about a happy ending for all concerned. The movie was great fun, and I'm happy to report that it translates pretty well to the stage too. Doubtless conscious of being a premiere and therefore setting a standard, directors Terese Dunne and Rosemary Winkless didn't hold back on making this show as spectacular as possible, and in most respects, their enthusiasm paid dividends. Their casting was strong, their direction of principals and the use of space for both principals and chorus was extremely impressive. The children, who obviously play a major role in the success of the show, were meticulously drilled yet still so full of energy and natural flow. They shone like little stars. Played on an empty stage, with neutral flats and a massive, and well-utilised, projection screen, the technical and visual aspect of the show was ever- so-slightly two-dimensional and might have benefitted from some solid scenery pieces. That said, the projections were excellent and varied, giving a good sense of location and atmosphere. Use of more different levels might have enhanced some of the pictures when a full chorus were on the stage. But the good choreography and very secure lighting plot did ensure that there was plenty of variety to savour. Lighting was generally very good and colourful, and only on one occasion was the main lighting at a level where it partially washed out the lower level of the projections. Good use of isolated spots and special area lighting. The sound was very good and nicely balanced, and with so many radio mics I'm delighted that none of the children's lines were missed. Mr Poppy possibly needed to be slightly boosted at the start of the show, but once he settled, the sound was fine. I love a keyboard that does the work of half an orchestra, and in the creative hands of Musical Director, Patrick Dunne, that's exactly what I got. With only himself and guitar and percussion, there was a full and robust output from the pit, which beautifully enhanced the on-stage activity. Vocal coach, Irene Dunne, had obviously done excellent preparation, with all her choruses making a tuneful, precise and secure vocal contribution to the musical success of the show. Great work was especially noted on the youngest stars, who performed their music most delightfully, even the rapper! The choreography of Terese Dunne, Tara Gill and Aoife Kerley, assisted by Nik Parks, Zoe Parks and Ellen Hodgers, was vibrant and varied. Good precise military movement for the Oakmoor kids, and flamboyant, energetic routines for the St Bernadette's mob. The adults too contributed to the spectacle, always on point and full of energy. The children's Nativity show numbers were so much fun. Taking the central role of Paul Maddens, was Brendan Cleary who captured the essence of the Grinch-like, rather sullen 'I don't really want to be here' teacher. He had delightful and emotional moments of hope and romance, but for the most part, his grumpiness was his defining feature and he played it with conviction. His timing was excellent, and his grumpy rapport with the school children was very natural. He also had a very good vocal quality. Mr Poppy is a role that gives a grown man the chance to become a big kid again, and the opportunity was grasped firmly by Tom Doonan in a fantastically funny manner. Basically, he's as silly as Mr Blobby, but without the costume to hide behind. The kids on stage loved him and so did the audience. As the catalyst for mayhem and madness, but also for the progression of the central love story, he played his role with total conviction, great comedy and good vocal security. Playing the female lead, Jennifer Love, Sheena Duffy had the warmth and sincerity required to be focus of Mr Maddens' affection. Brimming with expectations in her early scenes, she transformed nicely into the 'didn't quite make it' character, reflecting on how different things might have been. Sympathetically played, and with very nice vocals. Head teacher, Mrs. Bevan, was played with assurance and authority by Jane Stanley, yet vulnerable enough to be gently seduced by the attentions of the opportunistic Lord Mayor, played with good smarmy charm by Kevin Stanley. The wannabe Lord Olivier was perfectly captured by Andrew Brown as Gordon Shakespeare, with all the charm of a pantomime baddie. He was forthright, robust and appropriately sulky at ending up as a primary school teacher, instead of finding fame in Hollywood. With a fine singing voice, he made a hilarious impression playing 'Herod' in his own school's rock opera. Very good character performance. Lucie Robinson packed several punches as the acidic theatre critic, Pamela Burns, making the most of her opportunities to be a perfectly nasty piece of work, while Aoife Curran-Butler gave a convincing performance as the icy, high-powered Hollywood executive, Ms Parker. There was good support too from Siobhan Jordan, Tony Dolan, Aaron Duffy and EJ Dunne, in a variety of cameo roles, all performed with confidence and competence. And then there were the kids! The snotty- nosed posh kids from Oakmoor School were delightfully led by Arden Oakes as Sebastian, Mia Gogarty as Malificent and Noa Goss as Thomasina. As a group, they perfectly performed in a smug, superior manner, giving great expression to "Better Than You" and "Herod, the Rock Opera". Leading the way in St Bernadette's were dynamic performances from Tess Kierans, Noah Cotter, Brendan Carolan, Elliott McLoughlin, Brianna Little, Dearbhla Tuite, Emily Morgan, Clodagh Maloney and Alan McIntyre, each displaying excellent individual personalities, and giving 100% commitment to their roles. Their entire team were effervescent and adorable, with little Tess Kierans being especially cute in her solo work. Well done to each and every one of you.  And if two choruses of children weren't enough, there was also an adult chorus, whose contribution was always enthusiastic, and well-rehearsed. They also made a good vocal impression in their big musical numbers. Congratulations on a great display of costumes throughout the show. Principals were all dressed appropriate to their status; Mr Poppy wild and unkempt, Mr Maddens suitably square, Mrs. Bevan and Ms Parker suitably austere. The children's outfits were spic and span for Oakmoor, and nicely scruffier and more random for St Bernadette's. But the hard work was done on a great array of fancy outfits for the school shows, and for the early Christmas songs. Excellent work in these areas. Wigs, hair and make-up were all spot-on. I loved Mr Shakespeare's 'hard- rock' image for 'Herod'. I wouldn't be at all surprised if this show became a highly popular choice for companies that have a good youth section, and who like to present Christmas entertainment. It really is great fun. This production by SONG offered so much energy, presented so much talent, and delivered an excellent standard of entertainment to a very appreciative audience. SONG is a company that thrives and benefits from a perfect amalgamation of youthful energy and focused learning, and a wealth of experienced mentors. Their strength in depth is a sure guarantee that they will flourish in the future as well as the present. Thank you to all concerned for this thoroughly entertaining first taste of Christmas spirit this year.

Sister Act is a show that, with only a few characters on-stage for the first ten minutes, can take a while to warm up and get going, but once Deloris Van Cartier dons her habit and enters the convent, the fun and frolics and the fast-flowing sequence of joyful choruses never cease until the final curtain. Add to that some nice emotional moments and some outrageously silly gangsters, and this show is always going to entertain. In this production, a high standard of performers ensured that the slightly less successful technical aspects of the show didn't detract too significantly from the audience enjoyment. I did feel that attention to the technical side of the show was a bit disappointing. While the concept of the two revolving set pieces on stage was a good one, the artwork didn't really enhance them, being a bit untidy and abstract, with the notable exception of the abbey, which was nicely created, along with the good arches at the back of the stage. Good props did help to give each scene an identity of its own, but those revolves added little warmth to any of the settings. Neither was there much warmth created by the lighting, which was initially a little bland, but did improve significantly during the more joyous Abbey scenes. Stage manager, Clare Campbell, did, however, manage to keep the scene changes rolling fairly swiftly and smoothly. Sound quality was good, and the singers had no difficulty in being heard above the band. In all other respects, however, director/ choreographer, Mary McDonagh, presented us with a show that rattled along at a very good pace, had good emphasis on comedy and the realization of characters, was musically strong and was bright and breezy, choreographically. Her performers were never short on confidence or ability, and her chorus and dancers approached all their routines with good energy and a very impressive level of competence. The comedy of 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' was a high point of comedy, and a particularly good job was done on the second act reprise of 'Fabulous Baby', leading into a beautiful shaped and sung 'Sister Act'. Musical Director, Niamh Crowley, gave good leadership to a very accomplished orchestra, who maintained a strong and rhythmic accompaniment throughout the show. She had obviously prepared her chorus thoroughly, as evidenced by their good vocal contribution to the show. Likewise, all of the principals were in fine voice and secure in their music. It takes a formidable woman with a good set of lungs to fulfill the credentials of the leading role of Deloris Van Cartier, and in Sinead Conway, Sligo found such a woman. She had a commanding voice and presence and was a natural leader among the nuns. Her comedy was secure, and she had fun with her romantic encounters with Sweaty Eddie. Equally secure and confident was the austere and sometimes unorthodox Mother Superior, delightfully portrayed by Angela McGuire. A wealth of experience gifted her with very good comedic timing, and she really sold her 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' number. Fiona Hiney, in the role of Mary Roberts, got a very good contrast between her early shy and naïve scenes and her later determined and loyal friend, giving a strong rendition of 'The Life I Never Led'. Rebecca McGillen provided lots of laughs as the delightfully over-the-top cheerful nun, Sister Mary Patrick, and she blended well with the straight-talking, severe, but ultimately pleasant and comedic Sister Mary Lazarus, a role thoroughly enjoyed by Maureen Howley. Good support in the convent came from Siobhan Terry as Sr Mary Theresa, and Cath Rahilly as Sr Mary Martin of Tours. If Niamh Keaveney as Michelle and Aoibhinn Dooner as Tina seemed at tad young to be giving advice to Deloris, they nevertheless performed with confidence and credibility, secure in their vocals and light on their feet. The male cast was led by a very likeable and endearing Eddie Souther, played by Kieran Cunnane. With strong comic ability, and a pleasant voice, it was his sympathetic acting that made him a firm favourite with the audience. 'I Could Be That Guy' was nicely sung. Franny Curley was possibly a bit gentle as thug gang leader, Curtis Jackson, but he maintained his character well throughout and made a good job of 'When I Find My Baby'. The comedic trio of Joey, TJ and Pablo, played respectively by Killian Oates, Luke Devaney and Brian McGauran, gained many belly laughs from the audience, especially for their ridiculous antics during 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', which, for me, was the comedy highlight of the show. Joe Shannon gave a good account of himself as Monsignor O'Hara, although I did feel that he played his punch lines a tad too deliberately towards the audience. Ben O'Loughlin and Darren Jones gave good support in a few cameo roles, each of which had a good individuality. A good solid performance was given by the nun's chorus, who seemed to enjoy transitioning from a tuneless mob into a very tuneful and pleasing choir of angelic quality. Their robust vocals as the show progressed were most impressive. Neither did they lack energy in the execution of their routines, as they made the most of the rock and rap rhythms. They were enhanced on a few occasions by an enjoyable contribution from the altar boys, who also performed with gusto. While the nuns' habits were sufficient to represent that they were nuns, the chorus needed to take more care with how they presented themselves, some having their veil too far back, some with wimples tucked in, some visible. More uniformity would have advanced their visual appeal. As glitz and glamour was added, however, they became much tidier. Deloris, Michelle and Tina's outfits looked fabulous, baby! The gents were all suitably attired, with Sweaty Eddie's peel-off outfits working well during 'I Could Be That Guy'. This was a show with lively and energetic dances, some wonderful vocal displays, from principals and chorus, and some really excellent comedy sequences, all of which sent the audience, and this adjudicator, home with smiles on their faces and songs in their hearts. Thank you for the uplifting religious experience!

For those who, like myself, may be unfamiliar with the show, "First Date" is just that, a couple of hours in the company of a seemingly mismatched couple, on a blind date organised by a relative of the female. The couple and the barman are the only real characters on stage, while the remainder of the cast are a physical representation of the voices in the heads of the central couple. A sister, a mother, an ex-girlfriend, the voice of conscience, a bailout friend, contribute to the story in a series of often hilarious freezes, and occasionally perform together as commentators on the risks of blind dating. It really is a simple formula, but one that is very cleverly put together, and features some great musical numbers and quite brilliant comedic opportunities. On this occasion, all of those opportunities were taken in presenting a riveting night of rib- tickling hilarity. Any director taking on a premiere of an unknown show is putting themselves on the parapet, risking a hammering if the goods aren't delivered in a manor to encourage others to take up the challenge, but I'm very happy to acknowledge that Director Cian O'Dowd need have no worries of being chastised for his courage. In every respect, he realised the potential of this piece, with a no-nonsense, clean and simple set, effective and atmospheric lighting, and above all, eliciting comedic performances of the highest standard with a production that used verbal and the physical technique to make this a sparklingly dynamic vehicle. The show was played on basically a black box set, with nice overhead restaurant lights, ample appropriate furniture and good props, including consumable food and drinks. With the entire action occurring in the one space, there was little to trouble stage manager, Conor Kilduff, bar having props on stand-by and calling the lighting cues. There were no awkward moments at all in a seamless easy flowing presentation. One could, I suppose, have had a more detailed and 3-dimensional set for the restaurant, but I honestly doubt that it would have enhanced the show, the benefit of the black box being to focus attention on the performers rather than their surroundings. The lighting, as mentioned above was atmospheric and colourful, but also very disciplined, as much of the action centered around freezes, during which the 'voices in their heads' came to life. These freezes were beautifully timed and managed and were extremely effective. In such an intimate performance space, sound quality was of a high standard and perfectly balanced. This isn't a show that's big on choreography, but when the opportunity arose, choreographer Ainé Foley gave shape and style to her performers, adding some nice touches to the visual quality of the action. She was also blessed to have a group who were all very capable of good movement. I'm not a big fan of backing tracks, as they tend to be merciless and do not take into account faults, pauses, fluctuating tempos from singers. Therefore, the central task for Musical Director, Keelin Kilduff, was to have her performers so meticulously rehearsed that they would never falter. This, she achieved most successfully. All of her singers were well-drilled, beautifully harmonious and articulate with their diction. Each person on stage was appropriately attired to suit their personality, with the 'voices' being established in their different characters by the simple addition of a hat, or glasses or a scarf. Simple and effective costuming is one of the joys of a small cast show, I suppose. And as for the performers, Stuart Pollock, as Aaron, had enough nerdiness at the outset to suggest that he might not be the Mr Right that Casey was hoping to meet, but with great acting, excellent comedy and a fabulous vocal display, he became more appealing as the night progressed. This was a very disciplined and well-judged performance, with many outstanding moments, most notably when he eventually confronts his ex-girlfriend, and as he reacts to the letter that he was left by his mother. An excellent performance. Likewise, there was a great range of emotion expressed by a totally convincing Casey, expertly played by Jessie Woods. She had the perfect sharpness and wit for one who had played the field with the bad boys in the past, yet there was great heart and sentiment in her realisation that Aaron might just be what she needed to change her ways. Her singing was also top-notch. But it was the great balance between these two that was the cement that held the whole show together. Robust support came in the shape of Adam Trundle as the voice of Aaron's conscience, a role played with great comedic prowess and secure vocal quality. His timing was impeccable, and he was as physically funny as his delivery of lines. This was very good work, as was the contribution of Robert Gallagher, who, among his characterisations, shone at his brightest as Reggie, the deliciously over-the-top bail-out friend of Casey. He handled the 'you're either having a really good time, or you're dead in the back of a van' monologue with perfect delivery and sublime comedy. Shauna Maguire greatly impressed as Casey's pushy and impatient sister, but perhaps it was her role as Aaron's mother that was the most affecting. As with the other cast members, her versatility was wonderful, in acting, comedy and vocally. Aine Winter's greatest triumph was as Allison, Aaron's ex-girlfriend, which afforded her opportunities to display lust, passion, comedy and anguish and she performed each emotion with panache and yet another powerful vocal ability. Completing the cast was Philip Emmet as the waiter, a role that benefitted from his dry, wry delivery of his comedic lines. This was another wonderful performance that peaked with his compelling delivery of the very funny 'I'd Order Love'. But perhaps the greatest strength of this show was the combined efforts of the group, that infused the ensemble pieces with raw energy, perfect harmony and an overwhelming sense of camaraderie. Thank you to everyone involved for the top-notch production and for the belly laughs. This was what entertainment is all about. Thoroughly entertaining. Thank you also for the warm hospitality in the beautiful Riverbank Arts Centre.

It's been quite a while since I've had the pleasure of attending 'The Sound of Music', a show very close to my heart, having begun my theatrical involvement (a long time ago), playing Kurt in the Opera House in Belfast, while my father played Uncle Max. In Newcastle West, the memories came flooding back, as I enjoyed the wonderful musical score and the ever-popular story of Maria Reiner and the Von Trapp Family. The strength of this production lay in good performances from the central characters, and in a very capable and tuneful female chorus. While the technical side of the show was by no means a disaster, it is the area where, in future productions, perhaps more creativity in design would make better use of the available space. While the mountain back-drop created an impressive focal point, there was just too little scenery available to make a good distinction between the indoor and outdoor scenes at the Von Trapp home, and on occasions, the movement of some pieces seemed superfluous. The trellised flats either side of the stage were quite effective, except that they moved a lot, and seemed to impede the smooth entrance and exit of people and of other pieces. I do appreciate the lack of space that you had backstage, and the hard work the stage team did to keep everything moving, and to attempt to make the scenes as varied as possible. Directors Tom Madigan and Susan Brown kept very true to the book with this production, adding only the "I Have Confidence" solo for Maria, and swapping "Something Good" in place of "An Ordinary Couple", both changes of which I strongly approve. If there was a weakness in performance, it was perhaps that some of the principals needed to assimilate their reactions and tone of voice with what they were saying or singing, as on occasions, the dialogue came across as 'reading from a script' rather than coming from the heart. The notable exceptions to this were Maria and the Mother Superior, who flowed with a natural ability and with great confidence. The children were beautifully directed in their action and their delivery. Tara Downes proved to be the perfect choice for the role of Maria, with just enough mischief to accentuate her youthfulness, a bundle of compassion towards the children, a confident boldness to confront the Captain, and a very convincing inner conflict as she came to terms with discovering love for the first time. This was a very good complete performance, combined with a most pleasing vocal quality. Co-director, Susan Browne, led by example by giving a splendid performance as the Mother Abbess, filled with a religious devotion and a heart full of compassion. While her "Favourite Things" duet with Maria was of great quality, it was her "Climb Every Mountain" that really made a powerful impact. Very nicely delivered. Charlie O'Connell had the strong physical presence to present himself as a disciplinarian Captain, but was perhaps a little less comfortable with his relationships with Elsa and Maria. There was good sincerity in his anger at the intrusion of Nazi-Germany into his Austrian lifestyle, and also a nice warmth in his rendition of Edelweiss. Paul Moriarty was an amusing Uncle Max, trying to make the most of his comedy, if on occasions a tad too deliberate in his delivery. Molly Giltenane was similarly too exaggerated in her movement as Baroness Elsa, and while she looked and sounded perfect for the role, she needed to be a little less mobile and a little more relaxed. Their musical numbers together, however, were well-delivered and well received. A young Domhnall O'Connor gave good account of himself in creating the character of Rolf Gruber, sincere in his affections for Liesl, and conflicted in his acceptance of Nazism. "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" was very nicely presented. He was helped by an equally splendid performance from Keelan Fahy as Liesl, played with just enough attitude to capture the mischief of a teenager, but also with a bucket load of affection for her family. The children, from Friedrich through to Gretl, performed beautifully throughout the show. Joseph O'Connor and Padraig Doherty were delightfully pleasant young men, while Leah Walsh as Louisa, was convincingly precocious. Jade Massey's Brigitta was amusingly wise beyond her years, and Molly Sparling and Anna O'Sullivan added much cuteness to the junior roles of Marta and Gretl. The trio of nuns, Evelyn Shanahan as Sister Bertha, Caroline Daly as Sister Margareta and Ann Marie Murphy as Sister Sophia, gave good account of themselves in a nicely delivered "Maria" and maintained their characters well throughout the show. Dinny Ahern was a suitably treacherous Franz, the butler, and Caroline Walsh, was a very capable Frau Schmidt. Tom Madigan had the stature and menace to be a convincing Herr Zeller. Other minor roles were comfortably portrayed by Padraig O'Shea, Marie Hestor, Helen Ahern and Lisa Kelly. The Nuns Choruses were all very nicely sung, and they presented themselves well, if only they had looked a little more joyous, particularly when singing the celebratory Alleluia at the wedding. I was delighted that all the nuns pieces were sung in full, as the vocal quality was most satisfactory. They contributed well to the overall production. A more creative lighting plot might have enhanced the settings, like using break- up or leaf gobos for the garden scenes. As it was, the lighting succeeded in making sure that everyone was well-illuminated, and colour variations did help to change the atmosphere. Sound quality was generally good, although sound effects (Abbey bells, etc) needed to be faded down, rather than cutting off abruptly. Much more successful was the visual presentation, with very nice costumes for the children and the principals, and the nuns all looking proper and correct. The only glaring error, costume wise, is that Von Schreiber, as a high ranking Naval Officer, would most definitely not have been wearing a Nazi uniform. The children presented themselves very well at all times. The curtain outfits were very good. With a small band at his disposal, Musical Director, Michael Young, was perhaps a little heavy-handed on his keyboard, which occasionally competed with the singers on stage, but tempi were good and steady throughout the show. The principals all seemed to be musically well-rehearsed, with the Nuns Chorus sounding articulate and harmonious, and the children making a splendid job of their harmony pieces. There are very few opportunities for choreography in this show, but the children's numbers were kept interesting and well-devised, and they were performed with confidence and enthusiasm. The Sound of Music boasts a wonderful musical score, endearing characters and a great story of family and National pride in the face of adversity, and all of those elements were given such good treatment by a most enthusiastic and hardworking cast. I am grateful to have been there to have so many happy memories brought back to me. Thank you all for a most enjoyable and entertaining evening.

It never ceases to amaze me that the wonderful old chestnut, that is "Oklahoma!", still continues to captivate audiences and more significantly, that directors still manage to find novel ways to keep it fresh and individual. Such was the case with this beautiful production by Naas Musical Society. It says a lot about the class and talent of esteemed Director, Mona Conroy, that even on this, her swan song as a director, (such a sad revelation) she has infused this production with so many wonderful and original touches. The choreographed overture was delightful and nicely introduced the chorus and some of the principal characters even before a word had been spoken, which made a pleasant change from the usual opening scene with just three characters on stage for the first 10 or 15 minutes. The use of little children in this scene was also charming. Then there was the excellent strengthening of the relationship between Laurey and Gertie which gave a new dynamic to both of their characters and added some lovely comedic moments. The whole production had a feeling of inclusivity, with chorus introduced as observers and by-standers in several scenes, which I'm quite sure gave the chorus a greater sense of involvement. The pace of the show was well judged and there was good focus on the important pieces of action, although I did feel that Jud's death happened just a tad too swiftly. A bit more of a tussle might have intensified the drama before he fell on his own knife. But it has to be said that the overall production had the stamp of a lady who continues to inspire and encourage, whose positive influence will endure even in her absence and whose talent and expertise will be sadly missed if those very experienced boots are finally hung up. Thank you, Mona Conroy, not just for this production, but for your legacy. The set was well-designed and beautifully painted and presented. The backdrop was attractive, while the set pieces were securely constructed and nicely detailed, Aunt Eller's House and the Smoke-house making a fine impact. My only grumble was that there was no way to alter the appearance of the stage for the Box Social, which appeared to be held in Aunt Eller's yard. In every other respect, staging was visually strong and managed with comfort and precision by a well-drilled stage crew under the leadership of Stage Manager, Tom Kavanagh. There were some very authentic and appropriate props and furniture, although the hot-water bag and some of the... (ahem!) rather scant underwear items in Ali Hakim's bag were rather obviously a bit too modern. Lighting, throughout, was splendid, with good use of colour, nice atmospheres, and a fine level of surrealism for the dream ballet. The quality of sound was excellent, especially given that the orchestra were behind the stage. Balance and clarity were of the highest order. Curly was lucky not to lose a few fingers when his gun-shot was let off just a tad too prematurely in the smoke-house, but that's a very minor issue and was actually quite amusing. The choreography of Grace McGrath is consistently clean, precise and designed to suit and accentuate the talent of her choruses and dancers, which is why it achieves a high level of success. As with Mona Conroy's work, there is a sense of inclusivity, giving everyone their moment in the limelight, and saving her best work for those most capable of a challenge. The Dream Ballet was very well worked and featured good moments of fun combined with strong moments of drama. The Farmer and the Cowman was energetic and fluent and very well danced. Kansas City, as the opening choreographed number, was fun-filled and got things off to a confident start. Very good work. Hidden behind the set, the orchestra for this production were disciplined and precise and expertly led by Musical Director, Mairead McKenna. That the balance of sound was perfect and that entrances and exits, musically, were tight and accurately observed is testament to good preparation and thorough rehearsal. Chorus vocals were wonderful, and all of her principals were on cue and on point in their delivery. The show was musically delicious, and the familiar tunes were greatly enjoyed by the audience. Rory Dignam offered us a cocky, secure and very believable Curly, but also good in his sentimental romance with Laurey. He had good appearance, good confidence and a very pleasant voice. Beside him, Sarah O'Driscoll made an absolutely delightful Laurey.
