Director, Robert O'Neill, showed a good eye for detail with this show, with sets, costumes and lighting all working well together in presenting a very smooth and coordinated production. Characters were well-realised, and the action of the show flowed very naturally, with no uncomfortable moves or disruptions to the pace. The stage space was well utilised, and entrances and exits made sense. A very fine orchestra, situated behind the main set, and under the direction of Joan Butler, played the score with accuracy, good tone and tempi throughout. The good vocal harmonies, evident in all the choral pieces, were a testament to a well- rehearsed and drilled chorus, and indeed, there was very good musical security from all of the principals. The balance between the orchestra and the performers was just right, with every word perfectly audible. Siobhan Kavanagh was a most delightful and mature Elle Woods, the highlight of her performance being her emotional and sentimental scenes, which were acted with great sincerity. She had an excellent sense of comedy and a voice that was perfect for the demands of the role. She put great energy into her routines with the Delta Nu. Aidan Cooney made a wonderful transition from the shy but determined bookworm of his early scenes to the confident and honorable gentleman of his final encounters with Elle and with Callahan. He and Elle pitched their romance perfectly and with such sincerity. His vocal quality was also most impressive. Richard O'Toole, as Warner, was impressively insipid and spineless in character in contrast to his outward arrogant confidence, and extracted great comedy from his narcissism. A very well- played role with good vocal security. Mega-impressive was Kayla Kehoe in the role of Paulette. With wonderful facial expression, excellent body language, perfect comedic timing and a voice that ranged from mellow to mighty, this was a perfectly cast and perfectly played character. Barry Harmon was a decidedly sleazy and unpleasant Professor Callahan, commanding in his early scenes, delivering "Blood in the Water" with confidence, and then disturbingly creepy when he turned his attentions to Elle. Nicely played. Erin Hogan was deliciously condescending as Vivienne Kensington, with an iciness that contrasted beautifully with Elle's warmth. Her playing of the final scenes, when she sees the errors of her judgmental attitude, was very good indeed and strongly sung. Enid Hoops was given excellent character and personality by Niamh Kelly. Her timing was on point as she made the most of her visual and vocal comedy. Noreen Farrell as Margot, Róisin Currid as Pilar, Avril Lakes as Serena and Madeline Doyle as Kate, led the Delta Nu students with confidence, assurance and a great sense of fun. Each had a well-defined individuality, and collectively they were effervescent and energetic both in their vocals and in their movement. Madeline also put in a good contrasting performance as Chutney Wyndham in the courtroom. Riccardo Tavoliere served up a tasty beef- cake of a character as Kyle O'Boyle, very good with his comedy and very comical with his dancing. Choreographer, Tracy Rea, also played the role of fitness guru, Brooke Wyndham, and while part of her performance was diminished by a mishap with a radio mic, which affected her song and her skipping routine, she still displayed very good comedy and vocals and created a strong character. Good support came from Seán Óg Ferry as a self-confident Aaron Schultz, Aoife Doyle as both Sundeep Padamadan and Whitney, Tricia Millar as the Judge and the Store Assistant, Kieran Hutchinson as Elle's Father and Audrey Cooper as her mother. There were strong cameos from Lee Brennan as a very funny Nikos and Oisín O'Reilly as an equally funny Carlos. Oisín as did a fine job as Grandmaster Chad with a bit of good rapping. For the most part, Tracy Rea's choreography was high energy and very inventive, with particularly good routines for "Oh My God" and the majorette number. Indeed, all her routines were lively and very well-executed by an enthusiastic company, with the skipping routine being the only one that suffered due to technical hitches, but the intentions were good. Overall, the choreography contributed well to the success of the show, in no small part due to the chorus, who, as well as filing several other cameo roles, worked extremely well as a collective, producing good vocals throughout and executing their dance and movement efficiently and tidily. They were also very well involved in the action with good reactions and secure stage presence. Costumes were of a good standard and appropriate to each character, with Elle always looking elegant, and her besties always looking cool and youthful. Majorette outfits, especially Elle's, were great and hairstyles and make-up all seemed to blend it with the overall look of the show. I was afforded a warm welcome to the theatre and looked after very well by the friendly and efficient staff. This was a very lovely show, and thanks to all concerned for the wonderful entertainment. It was so nice to chat with some of you after the show.

Director Arthur McGauran had to cope with many cancelled rehearsals even in the days leading up to opening night in Naas, as the company was gripped by an unfortunate plague of Covid cases, but with fortitude and resilience, the passengers and crew of the S.S.American set sail as scheduled with a very tidy, secure and well-rehearsed production of Anything Goes. Arthur, both as director and as set-designer, had done a beautiful job of presenting the stage at its best, with nicely constructed and well-painted sets and with a very competent and capable cast of performers. The comedy of the show was pitched at a good level and the pace of the action was well-judged. Characters were well-realised and the overall production was just as it should have been, good light entertainment for entertainment's sake, and thoroughly enjoyable. The set made for smooth and efficient scene changes, with the main ships' deck being occasionally concealed behind well-constructed Bedroom trucks. Stage manager, Bob O'Kelly, kept everything ship-shape and ensured that delays were minimal. A nice touch was to open up the upper- deck to reveal the orchestra during Reno's cabaret numbers. Lighting and sound were both of a very good standard, the former using good area focus and nice atmospheric colouring of scenes, and the latter being well-balanced and employing good sound effects. Under Mairead McKenna's musical direction, we were treated to a beautiful accompaniment to Cole Porter's wonderful score, provided by a very competent orchestra and many beautiful vocalists. Harmonies were a strong feature of both the excellent quartet and the entire chorus, and were evidence of very good vocal preparation. Tempi and rhythms throughout the show were perfect. As Reno Sweeney, Dearbhail Downey led from the front, giving a strong character comedic performance, accompanied by a forthright vocal display. Her timing was very good, as was her stage presence. Daniel Ryan acted Billy Crocker very nicely, and sang with confidence, even if he occasionally looked in pain on his top notes. His comedy and his romance were well-realised. Sarah O'Driscoll didn't have enough occasions to display her lovely vocal quality, but she made the most of her opportunities, and played her role quite delightfully. Paul Dicker was an audience favourite in the role of Lord Evelyn Oakleigh, although for me, his comedy was a tad too pantomimed. Nevertheless, he was constantly animated and his rendition of The Gypsy in Me was very good. Andrew Docherty, by contrast, played Moonface Martin with subtle gestures, excellent tone of voice and immaculate comedic timing. This was a wonderfully funny performance, perfectly delivered. Charlene Masterson was a vibrant and sassy Erma, extracting good comedy and dynamism from an underwritten role. Very nicely played. Sean O'Keefe played Elisha Whitney with just the right amount of pomposity and a strong element of ridiculousness, resulting in a very fine overall performance. John Dooley made a good blustering Captain, ably supported by Rory Chadwick as a very competent and confident Purser. And then there was the crème de la crème of Naas Musical Society, the quite astounding and energetic Mona Conroy who, not contented with directing a lovely Oklahoma earlier in the season, donned her finery to deliver a beautifully played and timed comedic performance as Evangeline Harcourt. She's some woman for one woman! Very good support was given by the bevy of beauties that were Reno's Angels, Aishling Byrne, Ciara Dooley, Eimear Elsted, Maria Bergin, Sharon Ryan and Serena Salmon, who could all sing as well as they could pose and dance. Rick Kearns was a convincing Henry T. Dobson, Denis Kenny and Daniel Docherty got good comedy from the roles of Spit and Dippy, and Adrian King, John Bowdren, Peter Nolan, Dan Trundle and Mark Whelan all turned in fine cameo performances. Note-worthy were the vocal efforts of Adam Trundle, Dan Trundle, Mark Trundle and Shane Byrne as the very good Sailor Quartet. Millie Masterson stole the show as Cheeky. Grace McGrath used her main dancers (the angels) most effectively in all their numbers, and as the front-liners in the big choral numbers. Their routines were varied and classy and very well-executed. The chorus were also very capable in all their movement, adding depth to those big show-stopping numbers. There were some nice quirky moments in The Gypsy in Me, but perhaps more could have been done with the duets involving Bobby with Reno and Hope. They were always tidy, but perhaps a tad unadventurous. It was "Anything Goes" as the Act One finale, and "Blow, Gabriel Blow" where Grace's class got its best airing, benefitting from a chorus who were as energetic and animated as they were capable of producing excellent vocal harmonies. The show was very nicely costumed, with smart, tidy uniforms for the crew and appropriate fashions for the passengers. Reno and her angels were always radiant, and Evangeline must have had the classiest wardrobe on the liner. There was very good attention to the ladies' hairstyles, and make-up looked natural, with the angels having that noticeable hint of show-biz glamour. All-in-all, a nice eye- catching visual display, which extended beyond the footlights to include a very well-presented front of house, with an S.S. American photo booth, and a well- attired staff of crew-members. As I've come to expect from this lovely company, one is always guaranteed a certain standard of production and performance, a beautiful atmosphere, and a sense of pride in all their endeavours. Thank you sincerely for such an enjoyable end to my adjudication season.
